explainer: Diwali, the festival of lights, is celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists. It marks the victory of light over darkness and good over evil — most famously Lord Rama's return to Ayodhya after fourteen years of exile. Homes glow with diyas and candles as families share sweets and prayers.
name: Diwali

explainer: Holi, the festival of colours, welcomes spring across India and Nepal. It celebrates the divine love of Radha and Krishna, and the triumph of the young devotee Prahlad over the demoness Holika. Friends and families throw coloured powder and water in joyful celebration.
name: Holi

explainer: Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus Christ, observed by Christians around the world on 25 December. Traditions include church services, carols, decorated trees, feasts, and the exchange of gifts with family and friends.
name: Christmas

explainer: Eid al-Fitr, the Festival of Breaking the Fast, marks the end of Ramadan, Islam's holy month of fasting. Muslims gather for special morning prayers, share festive meals, and give charity (Zakat al-Fitr) so that everyone can join the celebration.
name: Eid al-Fitr

explainer: Eid al-Adha, the Festival of Sacrifice, honours Prophet Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice in obedience to God. It coincides with the Hajj pilgrimage; families share the sacrificial meal with relatives, neighbours and the poor.
name: Eid al-Adha

explainer: Guru Nanak Jayanti (Gurpurab) marks the birth of Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism and the first of the ten Sikh Gurus. Sikhs celebrate with early-morning processions, devotional hymns (kirtan), and free community meals (langar) served at gurdwaras.
name: Guru Nanak Jayanti

explainer: Vesak (Buddha Purnima) is the most sacred day for Buddhists, commemorating the birth, enlightenment and passing of Gautama Buddha — all traditionally on the same full-moon day. Devotees visit temples, meditate, and perform acts of kindness and generosity.
name: Vesak
